messages.subject: How to report model selection with WAIC
messages.subject_clean: How to report model selection with WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I posted this question on another group, but then found this one, and I think it is more appropriate here.

So, I fit multi-scale occupancy models in JAGS, and used R2jags to run the models. I calculated WAIC for model selection, following this approach:
https://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610036/thread/8211df61/#ea5c

I get a value for WAIC and deviance, where they state that ""deviance" is the deviance statistic for each observed node and "WAIC" is the corresponding WAIC penalty".

I also found this similar approach, but here the parameters are a bit different (waic and p_waic):
https://gist.github.com/oliviergimenez/68ad17910a62635ff6a062f8ec34292f

First, what is the proper way to report these values in a paper?

Second, I also tried the waic() function in the package "loo" but it doesn't work for an rjags object. Is there another way to use this function? Here I would be able to get  "elpd_waic", "p_waic" and "waic".

Thank you so much for any advice.
Cheers,
Ana

Hello friends and colleagues,

First of all, apologies for cross-posting, and for hijacking this list, but I think it may be of interest to some of you and perhaps you can help share this.

We are very pleased to once again announce that we are now accepting applications for our MSc in Statistical Ecology. This 1-year intensively taught MSc aims to give students

a sound understanding of the statistical foundations of modern methods in statistical ecology
knowledge and skills to use these methods effectively
experience of applying them to real-world problems, under the supervision of experts, some of whom are leading researchers in this field

It is taught by staff at the interdisciplinary Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM: https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/). The summer dissertation includes optional placements with collaborators in the UK or abroad, to give students experience of dealing with real-world problems in statistical ecology.

For any additional information, please direct enquiries to ma...@st-andrews.ac.uk.

Chris Sutherland

messages.subject: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model
messages.subject_clean: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Colleague Paula Ledezma and I, are analyzing Quetzal counts made over eight years in a Central-American location. We fit a year-stratified N-mixture model with a temporal trend on lambda (as described in chapter 2 of AHM2) and found a slight suggestion of an upward trend. Because the evidence is not overwhelming, it occurred to us that it would be interesting to let lambda vary randomly over time to see if the suggestion of an upward trend resurfaced in the randomly varying lambdas. And yes, we are aware that we could estimate one independent lambda per year for a similar inquiry, but we believe that enough biology is shared among years to justify a random temporal effect.

To build this random temporal effect, we added a random error term to the log(lambda) equation, with mean = 0 and sigma based on a uniform prior bounded by 0 and 2 (as in chapter 4 of Kéry and Schaub’s 2012 ‘BPA using WinBUGS’ book). The results are not good, it looks like the model has trouble converging on a variance (actually tau) for the random error term.

Has anyone seen this problem? We are finding it strange that no one seems to be putting random temporal effects on year-stratified N-mixture models. Is it dumb to try? Why?

Thank you for any feedback!

Gonçalo

messages.subject: Re: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model
messages.subject_clean: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Goncalo,

from what I understand I don't think you're doing anything wrong. But it may be that with only 8 years, a variance may be hard to estimate for the latent abundance. Also, using what some call "weakly informative" priors can often help with convergence. So, for instance, if the data say that a random year variance in log lambda is 0.25, then putting a U(0,1) prior may still be quite vague, but help getting convergence a lot. Another, even more "suggestive" prior in that case might be some more triangular distribution, such as a half-Cauchy (= t with 1 d.f.) or half-normal.

Best regards --- Marc

Subject: Introductory workshop on quantitative methods for population dynamics in R. June 1-2, 2023.

Introductory workshop on quantitative methods for population dynamics in R - second edition. June 1-2, 2023.

Quantifying population dynamics is crucial for the conservation and management of animal and plant species. This workshop deals with the analysis and modelling of population dynamics. In this introductory workshop, we will cover population projection matrix models, the estimation of demographic parameters (e.g. survival, dispersal) using capture-recapture models and the estimation of population density and abundance using capture-recapture, N-mixture and distance sampling models. The format of the workshop will be a combination of lectures and practical sessions in R with packages popbio, RMark and unmarked.

The workshop is online, free of charge, and will be video recorded. You just need to register here: https://forms.gle/FJmhhi9aSDpKWYRHA.

You may have a look to the material, video recordings and FAQs from the first edition of the workshop there: https://oliviergimenez.github.io/popdyn-workshop/.

Cheers,
Olivier Gimenez, Sarah Cubaynes and Aurélien Besnard.

messages.subject: What are the limitations of the Poisson/Poisson N-Mixture models?
messages.subject_clean: What are the limitations of the Poisson/Poisson N-Mixture models?
messages.body_plain:
In recent years I have been working with acoustic monitoring of bats. Such a method produces an exorbitant amount of data, but it is still difficult to obtain estimates of abundance and population trends because the number of recorded bat passes is a product of the population size by the vocalization rates of each individual - which is presumably greater than 1 in most cases.
In section 6.13.2 of the AHMbook, the authors introduce the Poisson/Poisson N-mixture model, which can estimate abundance in cases where detection rates are potentially greater than 1. Although the idea seems interesting to me, the authors point out that the models do not seem to produce sensible estimates of abundance in simulated data. Besides, there are few examples of their use in the literature (but see Nakashima, 2019, Population Ecology).
Therefore, I would like to understand a little more about the limitations of these models, and if there is already a more efficient alternative available for cases of multiple counting of the same individual.

messages.subject: Re: What are the limitations of the Poisson/Poisson N-Mixture models?
messages.subject_clean: What are the limitations of the Poisson/Poisson N-Mixture models?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Carlos,

I don't have much practical experience with the model and also note that it has not been applied a lot. Although: that latter may well be due in some part to the lack of its implementation in any of MARK, Presence, and unmarked.

While conceptually quite compelling as a model, I don't think it is very robust. Meaning, I think it can be hard to separate the two Poisson distributions just from the count data, especially, if you have "overdispersion" in one, the other, or in both processes.

A few years back I ran some comparative analyses (unpublished) on snow track counts of some mammal species, where the colleagues had different kinds of data, which let us fit the Poisson/Poisson, the Poisson/Binomial (i.e., the traditional Nmix) and (by reducing counts to DND) also a Poisson/Bernoulli (ie., RN) model. I remember that the P/P mix produced estimates that seemed way off for several of the species.

You can always try it of course and see "whether the results make sense". However, I would try to find ways in which you can add information about one or the other of the two processes. Or possibly use informative priors in a Bayesian analysis of such a model.

Best regards  --- Marc

Sent: Friday, February 10, 2023 16:13
To: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: What are the limitations of the Poisson/Poisson N-Mixture models?

In recent years I have been working with acoustic monitoring of bats. Such a method produces an exorbitant amount of data, but it is still difficult to obtain estimates of abundance and population trends because the number of recorded bat passes is a product of the population size by the vocalization rates of each individual - which is presumably greater than 1 in most cases.
In section 6.13.2 of the AHMbook, the authors introduce the Poisson/Poisson N-mixture model, which can estimate abundance in cases where detection rates are potentially greater than 1. Although the idea seems interesting to me, the authors point out that the models do not seem to produce sensible estimates of abundance in simulated data. Besides, there are few examples of their use in the literature (but see Nakashima, 2019, Population Ecology).
Therefore, I would like to understand a little more about the limitations of these models, and if there is already a more efficient alternative available for cases of multiple counting of the same individual.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to run a Bayesian Multistate Mortality model with 5 states. I have 52 individual fish tracked across 5 time steps. I am getting the error:

Error in jags.model(file = "model.txt", data = jags.data, inits = jags.inits, : Error in node y[6,2] Node inconsistent with parents.

I've read discussions in this group where folks have had similar errors, with it often being issues with the priors or initial values. However, I have adjusted priors and initial values, but am still running into the same error. The error is consistently with the same node, which makes me think it may be a simple formatting error somewhere. My code and data are attached and any help is greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

-Tyler

messages.subject: Modelling heterogeneity in stage-specific recapture probabilities in a multistate model
messages.subject_clean: Modelling heterogeneity in stage-specific recapture probabilities in a multistate model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all!

This is a question on the modelling of detection (recapture)
heterogeneity in specific states in multistate models. Some colleagues and I
are discussing which would be the most adequate way to model the case I
describe below. Any feedback will be appreciated!

Let's say we have a study population structured in
non-breeders and breeders. All individuals are marked as juveniles, and hence, non-breeders.
Our basic multistate matrix consists of three states: 1) Non-breeder, 2)
Breeder, and 3) Dead. Observations would then be 1) Seen as non-breeder, 2)
Seen as breeder, and 3) Not seen. Transition from a non-breeder to a breeder is
non-reversible and is not fixed at a specific age, but rather age-varying and
estimated by a recruitment parameter: (P(non-breeder at t --> breeder at t+1) =
Survival * Recruitment). Recapture probabilities are also different between non-breeders
and breeders.

However, here is where our particular case starts. Due to
the monitoring strategy used in the study population, there is a source of
detection heterogeneity present ONLY in breeders: breeders that have been
observed at least once are more likely to be observed in subsequent occasions,
while those that have become breeders but have not been observed yet may have
lower chances to be detected for the first time. I see this case as a sort of
"permanent trap-response".

We have some clear ideas on how to model this. One thing
that appears obvious to us is that the detection probability of breeders should
be split into two: the probability of observing a breeder for the first time (PB1)
and the probability to observe it in subsequent occasions (PB2). However, we are
doubtful about the right way to model this phenomenon in our state and
observation matrices. Note that we have prior information about PB1, but PB2
would be estimated inside the model. Here are a couple of ideas we had on how to
model this case of detection heterogeneity.

Option 1 is using an individual and time-specific binomial covariate
to deal with the situation. Because we know with certainty when the first observation
of a breeder occurs, we can use the covariate to indicate when PB1 and PB2
should be used. To exemplify how this may work, let me show an example where we
have an individual encounter history 1332333. The binary covariate for that
individual, with length 6 (number of occasions minus one), would take the sequence
000111, where 0 would “force” the use of PB1 (including the occasion at which
the individual is first observed), and 1 would “force” the use of PB2. Hence,
for the observation matrix row 2 (Breeder), column 2 (Seen as Breeder), the event
probability would be something like PB1*(1-cov[I,t]) + PB2*cov[I,t]. In the
example of an individual that has never been observed as a breeder, say, 1333333,
the covariate sequence would be 000000, since because the individual has never
been observed as a breeder, observation probability conditional on the individual
being an unobserved breeder would always be PB1. While this seems an intuitive
way to model this process, we also know that trap-response is a Markovian
process and because of this it is modelled in the state matrix. Hence, we have
some doubts about whether modelling the process in the observation matrix is an
adequate way to proceed or may cause some problems.

Option 2 would be to proceed by dividing the breeder state
in the state matrix into different states to account for trap-response, as is
commonplace in many designs to account for immediate trap-response. This would lead
us to a state matrix with 4 states instead of the initial 3, where states would
be something like 1) Non-breeder, 2) Breeder Not Yet Observed, 3) Breeder
Already Observed, 4) Dead. In this case, I understand that we should not
include PB1 (the probability of observing a breeder for the first time) as a
part of the transition between states 2 and 3, as we do know with certainty
when this transition happens (i.e., when a breeder is observed for the first
time), and then this transition is sort of deterministic, conditional on
survival. This may make our case different to the common modelling strategies
for trap-response scenarios.

There may be some other options we have not thought about.
However, I am especially interested in knowing whether any of both options
would be adequate. Any suggestions will be more than welcome. Thank you for taking
your time in reading this (long) post! I hope everything is clear and
understandable and otherwise do not hesitate to ask.

Have a nice day and many thanks in advance,

J.

This would lead us to a state matrix with 4 states instead of the initial 3, where states would be something like 1) Non-breeder, 2) Breeder Not Yet Observed, 3) Breeder Already Observed, 4) Dead. In this case, I understand that we should not include PB1 (the probability of observing a breeder for the first time) as a part of the transition between states 2 and 3, as we do know with certainty when this transition happens (i.e., when a breeder is observed for the first time), and then this transition is sort of deterministic, conditional on survival. This may make our case different to the common modelling strategies for trap-response scenarios.

There may be some other options we have not thought about. However, I am especially interested in knowing whether any of both options would be adequate. Any suggestions will be more than welcome. Thank you for taking your time in reading this (long) post! I hope everything is clear and understandable and otherwise do not hesitate to ask.

Have a nice day and many thanks in advance,

J.

> Betreff: Modelling heterogeneity in stage-specific recapture probabilities in a multistate model
>
>
> Hello all!
>
> This is a question on the modelling of detection (recapture) heterogeneity in specific states in multistate models. Some colleagues and I are discussing which would be the most adequate way to model the case I describe below. Any feedback will be appreciated!
>
> Let's say we have a study population structured in non-breeders and breeders. All individuals are marked as juveniles, and hence, non-breeders. Our basic multistate matrix consists of three states: 1) Non-breeder, 2) Breeder, and 3) Dead. Observations would then be 1) Seen as non-breeder, 2) Seen as breeder, and 3) Not seen. Transition from a non-breeder to a breeder is non-reversible and is not fixed at a specific age, but rather age-varying and estimated by a recruitment parameter: (P(non-breeder at t --> breeder at t+1) = Survival * Recruitment). Recapture probabilities are also different between non-breeders and breeders.
>
> However, here is where our particular case starts. Due to the monitoring strategy used in the study population, there is a source of detection heterogeneity present ONLY in breeders: breeders that have been observed at least once are more likely to be observed in subsequent occasions, while those that have become breeders but have not been observed yet may have lower chances to be detected for the first time. I see this case as a sort of "permanent trap-response".
>
> We have some clear ideas on how to model this. One thing that appears obvious to us is that the detection probability of breeders should be split into two: the probability of observing a breeder for the first time (PB1) and the probability to observe it in subsequent occasions (PB2). However, we are doubtful about the right way to model this phenomenon in our state and observation matrices. Note that we have prior information about PB1, but PB2 would be estimated inside the model. Here are a couple of ideas we had on how to model this case of detection heterogeneity.
>
> Option 1 is using an individual and time-specific binomial covariate to deal with the situation. Because we know with certainty when the first observation of a breeder occurs, we can use the covariate to indicate when PB1 and PB2 should be used. To exemplify how this may work, let me show an example where we have an individual encounter history 1332333. The binary covariate for that individual, with length 6 (number of occasions minus one), would take the sequence 000111, where 0 would “force” the use of PB1 (including the occasion at which the individual is first observed), and 1 would “force” the use of PB2. Hence, for the observation matrix row 2 (Breeder), column 2 (Seen as Breeder), the event probability would be something like PB1*(1-cov[I,t]) + PB2*cov[I,t]. In the example of an individual that has never been observed as a breeder, say, 1333333, the covariate sequence would be 000000, since because the individual has never been observed as a breeder, observation probability conditional on the individual being an unobserved breeder would always be PB1. While this seems an intuitive way to model this process, we also know that trap-response is a Markovian process and because of this it is modelled in the state matrix. Hence, we have some doubts about whether modelling the process in the observation matrix is an adequate way to proceed or may cause some problems.
>
> Option 2 would be to proceed by dividing the breeder state in the state matrix into different states to account for trap-response, as is commonplace in many designs to account for immediate trap-response. This would lead us to a state matrix with 4 states instead of the initial 3, where states would be something like 1) Non-breeder, 2) Breeder Not Yet Observed, 3) Breeder Already Observed, 4) Dead. In this case, I understand that we should not include PB1 (the probability of observing a breeder for the first time) as a part of the transition between states 2 and 3, as we do know with certainty when this transition happens (i.e., when a breeder is observed for the first time), and then this transition is sort of deterministic, conditional on survival. This may make our case different to the common modelling strategies for trap-response scenarios.
>
> There may be some other options we have not thought about. However, I am especially interested in knowing whether any of both options would be adequate. Any suggestions will be more than welcome. Thank you for taking your time in reading this (long) post! I hope everything is clear and understandable and otherwise do not hesitate to ask.
>
> Have a nice day and many thanks in advance,
>
> J.

messages.subject: Variable survey duration to estimate detection
messages.subject_clean: Variable survey duration to estimate detection
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
I am trying to find published examples of authors using variable length species occurrence/abundance surveys to account for imperfect detection, but I can't seem to figure out the right keywords to search under.. The type of analysis I'm imagining is similar to time-removal sampling or time-to-detection surveys, but instead of stopping at the first detection, observers just record the full length of the survey. The dataset would be species occurrence 0/1 and the amount of time the observer spent conducting the survey.
Can anyone help point me in the right direction of publications, or is there an obvious term for this kind of survey design that I just don't know?
Thank you for any advice,
Erica

messages.body_plain:
Dear Erika,

I don't think what you have in mind is that "special"/risky that you need to cite some antecedents. As soon as we go from designed surveys, such as BBS's, to the wild and wonderful world of mass-participation citizen-science surveys we always have variable survey duration, area, length etc. If you want to find examples of how people accommodate this in an analysis, perhaps look for some analyses done with eBird data. Clearly, survey duration should be incorporated as a covariate or as an offset.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: Variable survey duration to estimate detection
messages.body_plain:
Dear Erica,

for a dynamic occupancy model with single visits, Peach et al. (JAPPL, 2017) give a formulation that uses a measure of effort (such as survey duration) and a per-1-unit-detection probability to get the combined detection probability for the entire survey length. This may an interesting starting point.

In general, continuous-time formulations of such models may also be useful for what you seem to have in mind. For instance, for an occupancy model again, you could express binary detection or non-detection (actuall, "ever detected" or "never detected") during a time interval T as 1 - exp(T*lambda), where lambda is the rate of a Poisson point process in time that describes the number and timing of detections (I ​*think* I got that right with T in the product...​.). Ken Kellner and colleagues have done some recent work on occupancy models with continuous-time (CT) observation process:  https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13253-021-00482-y

With camera traps, ARUs and other data-logging devices one can bet that CT formulations of these models will become more important in the future.

Best regards  -- Marc

Without knowing the details of the data you are using I cannot be sure if this is the right answer for you, but the QPAD approach developed by Peter Solymos for use with bird data collected with variable sampling protocols might be an option. See his MEE paper for a description: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12106.

Peter has also put together a lot of documentation (e.g., https://peter.solymos.org/qpad-book/), along with an R package, and there are quite a few papers published with it (e.g. https://academic.oup.com/condor/advance-article/doi/10.1093/condor/duaa007/5838075).

I imagine if there is a constant rate of detection, and a known duration of survey we can estimate a true state and detection probability. I've seen the time to detection analyses as hierarchical models, but ebird, for example, doesn't have time to detection or time of first detection, rather only total survey duration. I'd like to formulate that as a hierarchical model!
> Do you know of hierarchical ebird analyses that use time (rather than repeat visits)?
> Thank you!
>
> On Fri, Feb 17, 2023, 2:09 AM Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

> > I don't think what you have in mind is that "special"/risky that you need to cite some antecedents. As soon as we go from designed surveys, such as BBS's, to the wild and wonderful world of mass-participation citizen-science surveys we always have variable survey duration, area, length etc. If you want to find examples of how people accommodate this in an analysis, perhaps look for some analyses done with eBird data.
